Old_Answer: I assume you mean “multiple different architectures” as opposed to “multiple different devices.” We're long past the days when each computer was unique by about 75 years, give or take. Assembly language isn't one language. Rather, it's the human readable form of the machine code for a particular processor architecture family. Each family has its own instruction set. There may be many different mutually incompatible dialects of assembly code for the same instruction set. For example, look up MASM and AT&T syntax for x86 assembly code. The Z80 is largely backward compatible with the 8080; however, because Intel® copyrighted* their instruction set, Zilog developed their own mnemonics and syntax. (*It’s unclear whether that copyright claim was meaningful.) In fact, you can even have incompatibility within the same assembly language dialect for the same processor family. Newer family members may support instructions and registers that aren't present on older family members, for instance. Instructions for newer processors won't work on older processors that lack those extensions. Now, there have been some assembly translators. It works best when the architectures involved are related, and the newer one takes translation into account. 8080 → 8086 is a famous example. These translators are rare. C code, on the other hand, can be compiled for whatever target architectures the compiler supports. As long as you stick to certain rules and build the right abstractions, it's not that difficult to write portable C code. All you need is a compiler for whatever target architecture you're interested in, and in many cases you are in good shape. It does take effort and care. It's orders of magnitude more approachable than porting large piles of assembly language though. Addendum Since it came up in discussion on a different answer, I figured I would mention it here.
